Rajasthan’s Luxury Hotels Turn to Solar, Water Recycling and Local Sourcing to Cut Carbon Footprint

31 Oct 2026, 11:15 AM IST · GlobeWire Daily Science Desk · Source: news.abplive.com

Image: Somrita Ghosh — Creative Commons

Key takeaways Sustainable Operations at ITC Rajputana On a sweltering weekend in Jaipur, when temperatures topped 40 °C, the ITC Rajputana hotel was operating at roughly 50 % occupancy. Chief Engineer Siddharth Bisht explained that the property runs a 250 KLD sewage‑treatment plan

Sustainable Operations at ITC Rajputana

On a sweltering weekend in Jaipur, when temperatures topped 40 °C, the ITC Rajputana hotel was operating at roughly 50 % occupancy. Chief Engineer Siddharth Bisht explained that the property runs a 250 KLD sewage‑treatment plant (STP) and a 30 KLD effluent‑treatment plant (ETP) every day, regardless of guest numbers. Treated water is reused for landscaping, cooling‑tower make‑up and toilet flushing, eliminating the need for fresh‑water intake for these functions.

The hotel also claims the only LEED Zero‑Carbon certification in Rajasthan. Its energy mix includes 2.5 MW of captive wind power from ITC’s Jaisalmer wind farms and a 100 kW rooftop solar array. According to Bisht, the wind and solar generation are “clubbed with the electricity supply” and power electrical boilers, heat pumps and the hotel’s HVAC system.

Architectural Passivity at Brij Laksham Sagar

In the Pali district, the heritage resort Brij Laksham Sagar has retrofitted a 19th‑century hunting lodge with thick mud‑stone walls, high‑thermal‑mass rooms, shaded verandas and natural ventilation. These passive design features reduce reliance on mechanical cooling. The resort currently draws electricity from the grid and uses motor‑driven water heating; a solar installation is being evaluated but not yet committed.

Solar‑Heavy Model at Dev Vilas, Ranthambhore

Owner‑operator Balendu Singh’s Dev Vilas eco‑resort in Sawai Madhopur sources about 62 % of its electricity from on‑site solar panels. The property harvests rainwater, recharges groundwater, and recycles treated water for non‑potable irrigation. Architectural choices – high ceilings, wide verandas and the absence of a central cooling plant – keep electricity demand low. Only 12 of the 28 rooms have heat‑pump units, which are switched on only when all 12 are occupied.

Context: Energy Use and Emissions in Rajasthan’s Hospitality Sector

The state lists more than 7,000 hotels, with over 3,000 registered on the Ministry of Tourism’s SAATHI portal. Global estimates suggest a typical hotel room consumes about 25 kWh of electricity per day, covering HVAC, lighting, appliances and minibar use. For 5‑star properties, the figure rises to roughly 118 kWh per room‑night. A 1.5‑ton air‑conditioner operating eight hours a day emits 2.2–3.6 kg CO₂ daily. Overall, an average hotel night generates ~35 kg CO₂, while a 5‑star night can emit 60–90 kg CO₂.

Practical Implications for Guests and Operators

  • Water security: Recycling 250 KLD of sewage and 30 KLD of effluent means the ITC Rajputana can sustain its landscaping and cooling needs without tapping additional groundwater – a critical advantage in Rajasthan’s “dark zones” where aquifers are depleted.
  • Carbon reduction: Wind and solar contributions at ITC Rajputana offset a portion of the hotel’s electricity demand, directly lowering the 60–90 kg CO₂ per room‑night typical of luxury hotels.
  • Cost considerations: Installing a 100 kW solar plant can cost ₹35–45 lakh; adding battery storage pushes the price to ₹60–90 lakh. Recent MNRE rules requiring domestically produced solar cells may raise these costs by ~30 %.
  • Employment stability: Brij Laksham Sagar shuts down during the peak summer months for maintenance, but staff receive full pay and are redeployed to a hill property, preserving income.
  • Local economies: Brij Laksham Sagar reports that ~70 % of its operational spend stays within a 10 km radius, supporting farmers, artisans and shepherds.

Outlook: Financing the Green Transition

Hotel chains are eyeing ESG‑linked financing such as green bonds, but India’s market lacks a dedicated domestic investor base. SEBI’s BRSR mandate pushes listed hotels toward higher ESG scores, yet the higher compliance costs and limited pricing advantage make green‑bond issuance a slow‑moving prospect for many operators.
